Precious Metals Quarterly 1Q2007 Silver # Silver ## Recent trends: high prices weakening outlook It has not broken any fresh new highs, the highest London fix in the first quarter of this year being $14.58/oz (on 26th February) compared with $14.94/oz in May last year. However, the London fix never fell below $12.21/oz in January-March, a feat (a low for a quarter) that has not been achieved since the fourth quarter of 1980 (towards the end of the Hunt Brothers’ market corner) in nominal terms, and since the second quarter of 1984 in real terms. And this has left the average for the first quarter of this year at $13.29/oz, the highest since the first quarter of 1981 in nominal terms, and the highest since the second quarter of 1984 in real terms. As in the early 1980s, high prices are again doing what economics would suggest. Demand is being dampened and supply is being encouraged. - Demand remains restrained by high prices. For the moment, silver’s use in jewellery and silverware is weak and demand from the imaging sector continues to be eroded. Silver’s use in electronics and electrical applications continues to grow well, but development of other uses is being hindered by today’s prices. We therefore find it hard to see silver consumption growing much on a net basis during this decade. - In contrast, mine supply looks set to increase by over 40% this decade. Primary silver mining is increasing, but the lion’s share of the growth is stemming from by-product output from zinc-lead, copper and gold mining. Mine supply grew by almost 40% in 1975-1985 in response to high silver prices. Silver averaged $11.55/oz in 2006, which is just 63% of the average during this period in real terms. However, the value of all metals produced at a typical silver-lead zinc mine in 2006 was two and a half times greater than the average for the period in real terms. - The combination of demand struggling to grow and massive additional mine supply will maintain significant market surpluses during our forecast period. We continue to expect these to eventually take prices lower, just as extra supplies of other metals will reduce the price of these. With this in mind, we forecast mine supply growth falling back by 2011. This will moderate the market’s surplus and halt further increases in the stock ratio. A comfortable, but not excessive, stock position should hold prices around long-run levels. However, a prolonged period of high prices for all metals run the risk of prompting even greater supply growth than we forecast. This will result in significantly higher stock build. Exploration, and evaluation of projects, for all metals is booming. The argument that silver's largely byproduct status makes supply relatively price inelastic has merit. But it w orks both w ays. High zinc, lead, copper and gold prices are also to result in higher silver mine supply. Further future silver mine supply is now committed. Most importantly, GoldCorp is proceeding w ith Penasquito. This w ill increase Mexican output even more, and w ill make GoldCorp the fifth largest silver miner in 2011 (third largest in 2010). The grow th in mine supply in the next few years w ill just about be unprecedented by historical standards. The market certainly needs no more further grow th beyond 2010, but current activities could surprise us even more. Precious Metals Quarterly 1Q2007 Silver 71 ## Forecast update: gets worse every time we look Perhaps the above title is a little harsh, but today’s high metal prices are conspiring to make tomorrow’s silver market considerably weaker. It is becoming increasingly difficult for us to envisage a strong market towards the end of this decade. Certainly, no one in the market, aside from the most fervent silver bulls, can envisage prices being anywhere near as high as they are today. Supply-side developments are easy to identify, but damage to silver’s demand-side prospects will take years to unwind. The demise of silver’s use by the imaging sector has been well documented. “Photographic” demand has been in decline since peaking in 1999, but digital technology was already eroding silver’s consumption prospects in photography for the whole of the 1990s. Digital technology did exist then, but its uptake, like for many things, was slow. Of course, the impact of the erosion of silver’s use in photography on the silver market is not as great as what it may seem at first. The lion’s share (traditionally over 90%) of secondary refined silver stems from photography. This share has historically fallen during periods of high prices because a wave of scrapping of je

wellery and silverware (and old coins) is encouraged.  And a significant proportion of silver “consumed” in photography is recovered.  Over half of silver consumed in photography has been in colour film and paper, and this is all lost to developing solutions for recovery.  Of the remainder of silver consumed in photography, around 50% of the silver is lost to the developing solutions.  Some developing solutions are discarded and recycling does involve some loss, and so not all silver lost to developing solutions is recovered.  The erosion of silver’s use in photography has therefore resulted in very little growth in scrap supplies overall in recent years.  It isn’t falling in line with silver’s use in photography because it has been taking time for years of photo-finishing and photo-capital scrap to by recycled.  Medical x-rays are an example. 

The silver industry has thus been very active in encouraging the development of new uses for silver, e.g. its anti-bacterial uses that have been known for a long time.  However, this use, and the development of others, is being hindered by today’s high silver prices.  Offtake for jewellery and silverware has also been hit and, while prices are high, competing discretionary luxury items are being marketed heavily.  Will demand for silver jewellery and silverware fully recover when prices eventually retreat? 

Although silver’s use in electronic and electrical applications is growing strongly, it is unlikely that global silver consumption will exceed its 2000 peak until not much before the end of this decade.  Thus, silver consumption will have barely grown on a net basis for a whole ten years.  In that time, silver mine supply is likely to have grown by over 40%.  We may in fact under-estimate the number of projects that could be supplying by then.  Of course, the market did and does need extra mine supply.  Above ground stocks were drawn down during the 1990s and early 2000s to reach a level equivalent to not much more than one year of consumption in 2003-2004 (having peaked at the equivalent of over five years in the 1980s).  Moreover, scrap supplies are being increasingly constrained by the erosion of silver’s use in photography, and thus mine supply must increasingly reflect total global demand. 

The scale of mine supply growth is already significant and is due, on the basis of our forecasts, to lift above ground silver stocks to the equivalent of 1.7 years of consumption by

2011.  Such stock levels could arguably be described as comfortable.  One year’s consumption is, after all, a tight market for silver.  And we argue that the easing in availability will take prices to $7.00-7.50 per ounce, which will be around silver’s long-run price in that year.  Persistent strong investor buying may hold prices higher and this will only serve to worsen silver’s fundamental position and maintain a market surplus.  At the moment, we expect the rapid growth in mi

ne supply to give out in 2011. This should help to hold prices around that point. However, if market fundamentals (including continued persistent investor buying) conspire to maintain sizeable market surpluses from that point, the silver market looks set for a repeat of the final quarter of the last century. High prices encouraged an increase in stocks (investor buying increased prices) in the late 1970s. High stocks ultimately unnerved investors in the early 1980s and buying stopped. Prices then fell during the late 1980s and remained below long-run prices (around $6.50/oz in today’s money) until 2004 as stocks were drawn down and sold. However, the flurry of new supply (and the prospect of even more new projects than we account for) runs the serious risk of creating casualties if the past is to serve as a guide. Mine supply grew by almost 40% in 19751985, but by just 8% in 1985-1995 (it fell 4% in 1990-1995). Several silver mining companies went bankrupt in this period. At the moment, the silver market should be healthy at the end of our forecast period, but any significant further increases in mine supply (and hindered demand) will take years to unwind. The further stocks rise, the longer it will take them to fall, and mine closures will likely have to ultimately ensue to help correct the market. After all, the market’s last stock-build took fifteen years to unwind although, admittedly, the last five years of that period involved taking the market from a comfortable to tight stock position.
